Newborn fawns of Mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) weigh approximately 2,950 grams [Wwb = approximately 2,950 grams] at parturition, a mass that reflects the species' strategy of producing a single precocial neonate after an extended gestation period. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of summer ranges in this species, where ambient temperatures frequently reach 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the dam's physiological state influences foetal development. During the organogenesis phase, the gestating embryo relies entirely upon maternal thermoregulation. These newborn individuals, often called fawns, display a spotted coat that provides cryptic camouflage against predators. The initial body mass is crucial for thermoregulation and early survival, as fawns must contend with fluctuating environmental conditions during their first weeks of life. Comparative observations among related cervids indicate that this birth weight is consistent with the altricial-precocial continuum observed in other members of the family Cervidae.

The adult body mass of Mule deer exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an average ultimate wet weight of approximately 90,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 90,000 grams] at full maturity. Males, by contrast, achieve a substantially larger adult body mass of roughly 150,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 150,000 grams], a difference that reflects the energetic demands of antler growth and intrasexual competition during the breeding season. These sexually mature adults maintain their body condition through seasonal cycles of forage abundance and quality. The reproductive strategy of this species involves a single annual birthing event, with most females producing one fawn per year [Ri = one fawn per year], although twinning can push the average closer to approximately 1.5 fawns per year [Ri = approximately 1.5 fawns per year] under favorable conditions.

From a developmental perspective, weaning represents a critical transition for Mule deer young. The wet weight at weaning averages 23,100 grams [Wwx = 23,100 grams], marking the point at which the fawn achieves nutritional independence from the lactating female. At the typical summer temperatures of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] that prevail on their summer ranges, the time since birth at weaning is roughly 132 days [tx = roughly 132 days]. This period of milk dependency allows the nursing offspring to build substantial body reserves before transitioning entirely to solid forage. The weaning process coincides with the late summer period when high-quality browse is still abundant. The initial growth trajectory of the fawn is remarkably rapid, with daily mass gains that enable it to nearly octuple its birth weight by the time nursing ceases. This nutritional emancipation is a gradual process, with fawns beginning to sample vegetation several weeks before complete cessation of suckling.

Sexual maturation in Mule deer occurs relatively late compared to many other ungulates of similar body size. Under thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which represent the upper end of their active metabolic range during summer, the time since birth at puberty is achieved at approximately 478 days [tp = approximately 478 days]. This delayed onset of reproductive maturity is characteristic of the species' life-history strategy, allowing individuals to allocate resources toward continued somatic growth before initiating reproductive effort. The first ovulation in females typically occurs during their second autumn, although some individuals may not breed until their third year depending on nutritional condition. Males reach testicular descent and begin producing viable spermatozoa at a similar age, though social dominance hierarchies often prevent young males from successfully breeding until they achieve larger body size. This extended juvenile period contributes to the species' relatively low annual reproductive output.

The maximum lifespan of Mule deer under natural conditions, measured at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is approximately 8,030 days [am = approximately 8,030 days], equivalent to roughly 22 years. Senescence in this species is characterized by gradual tooth wear, declining body condition, and reduced reproductive output in older females. The gestation period lasts about 207 days [tg = about 207 days] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a duration that synchronizes parturition with the spring flush of high-quality forage. This timing ensures that the neonate enters a resource-rich environment conducive to rapid growth. Field records from long-term studies indicate that very few individuals attain the maximum potential lifespan, as predation, harsh winters, and vehicle collisions impose substantial mortality, particularly on dispersing yearlings. The interplay between reproductive timing and environmental seasonality has been a central focus of life-history research on this species, with researchers emphasizing the adaptive significance of a relatively short gestation relative to body size.
